text: And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.
reflection: The very first promise of a Savior came in the darkest moment of human history. Adam and Eve had just disobeyed God, and sin had entered the world. Yet before God spoke of the consequences, He spoke to the serpent: "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel." A descendant of the woman would come and crush the serpent's head, though He would be wounded in the process. This was the first glimmer of the gospel. Christ would come, born of a woman, to defeat evil at the cost of His own suffering. As we begin this Advent season, remember that God's plan to save us began immediately after our fall. He did not wait. He did not abandon us. From the very beginning, He promised victory. Today, rest in the God who answers our failure with a promise. The Savior was coming, and He came.
question: What failure in your life could you see in the light of God's first promise of a Savior?
prayer: Lord, You answered our very first failure with a promise. Thank You that You did not abandon us. Help me rest in the victory of the Savior You sent. Amen.

text: And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because thou hast obeyed my voice.
reflection: After Abraham's great test of faith on Mount Moriah, God renewed His promise: "And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because thou hast obeyed my voice." Through Abraham's family, blessing would flow to every nation on earth. Not just one people, but all peoples. This promise was ultimately fulfilled in Jesus, the descendant of Abraham through whom salvation came to the whole world. The Christmas story is not just for one culture or country. It is good news for every tribe, language, and nation. The child born in Bethlehem came to bless people from every background. This is one of the beautiful threads running through Scripture: God's heart has always been for the whole world. As we celebrate this Advent season, remember that you are included in this promise. Whatever your background, the blessing of Abraham reaches you through Christ. And it calls you to share that blessing with others.
question: How could you share the blessing of Abraham, which reaches you through Christ, with someone else?
prayer: Lord, thank You that in Abraham's seed all nations are blessed, and that the blessing reaches me through Christ. Help me share that blessing with others this season. Amen.

text: I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth.
reflection: A pagan prophet named Balaam was hired to curse Israel. But instead, God put words of blessing in his mouth, including this remarkable prophecy: "I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel." Balaam saw a coming King, far off in the future. A Star and a Sceptre, symbols of royalty and rule. Centuries later, wise men from the East followed a star to Bethlehem, seeking the newborn King. God had kept His promise. There is something beautiful about this prophecy coming from an unlikely source. God can speak through anyone, and His purposes cannot be stopped. Even attempts to curse His people turn into blessing. As we wait this Advent, remember that God's promises often unfold slowly, seen from far off. But they always come to pass. The Star rose. The King came. Look to Him today.
question: Which of God's promises have you seen only from far off, and how can you keep looking to Him?
prayer: Lord, Your promises often unfold slowly, but they always come to pass. The Star has risen and the King has come. Help me keep looking to Him today. Amen.

text: The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken…
reflection: Moses spoke to Israel near the end of his life, promising that God would send another prophet: "The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken." Moses had been the great prophet who spoke God's words to the people. But he would not live forever. God promised that another would come, one like Moses, who would speak with God's authority. And the people were told to listen to Him. In the New Testament, the apostles declared that Jesus is that promised Prophet. He speaks the very words of God. Even more, He is the Word of God made flesh. At His transfiguration, the Father said, "hear ye him." This Advent, as we prepare for Christmas, the call is the same: listen to Jesus. Many voices compete for our attention during this busy season. But the promised Prophet has come. Take time today to read His words and hearken to Him.
question: Among the many voices of this busy season, how can you take time to hearken to Jesus?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the Prophet Moses promised. Quiet the many voices around me this season, and help me listen to Your words and follow them. Amen.

text: And when thy days be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom.
reflection: King David wanted to build a house for God. But God turned it around and promised to build a house, a dynasty, for David: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom." In the following verses, God promised that this kingdom would last forever. David's descendants would rule, and one of them would reign eternally. For centuries, Israel waited. Kings came and went, and eventually the throne was empty. It seemed the promise had failed. But then an angel appeared to a young woman named Mary and said her Son would receive the throne of His father David, and of His kingdom there would be no end. God had not forgotten. The everlasting throne belongs to Jesus. This Advent, take heart if some promise of God seems to have failed. His timing is not ours. What He promises, He fulfills, even if it takes centuries. The King of David's line has come.
question: Is there a promise of God that seems to have failed, and how can His timing give you hope?
prayer: Lord, You kept Your promise to David, even when it took centuries. When Your promises seem slow, help me trust Your timing. The King of David's line has come. Amen.

text: I will declare the decree: the LORD hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee.
reflection: Psalm 2 describes the nations raging against God and His anointed King. But God is not threatened. He declares His decree: "the LORD hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee." The King is God's own Son. This psalm is quoted in the New Testament to describe Jesus. He is the anointed Son, appointed by the Father to rule. At His baptism and transfiguration, the Father's voice echoed these words. And His resurrection declared Him to be the Son of God with power. The world may rage, but God's King cannot be overthrown. This brings peace in turbulent times. Nations rise and fall. Leaders come and go. Headlines can feel chaotic. But God's anointed Son reigns. As we prepare to celebrate His birth, remember that the baby in the manger is the eternal Son, appointed by the Father to rule over all. Bow before Him today. And rest in the knowledge that His kingdom is unshakable.
question: How can you bow before the eternal Son today and rest in His unshakable kingdom?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the Son of God, appointed to rule over all. I bow before You today, and I rest in the knowledge that Your kingdom cannot be shaken. Amen.

text: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre.
reflection: Psalm 45 is a royal wedding song, but in the middle, it addresses the King in astonishing terms: "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre." The King is called God. His throne is eternal. His rule is righteous. Hebrews quotes this verse and applies it directly to Jesus, showing that He is greater than the angels. He is the eternal King whose reign never ends and whose rule is always right. Earthly rulers often disappoint. Even the best leaders have flaws, and their reigns come to an end. But Jesus is different. His throne is forever. His sceptre is right. He will never abuse His power or rule unjustly. Everything He does is good. This Advent, as we look toward the manger, remember who lies there. Not merely a sweet baby, but the eternal King. Bring Him your loyalty and trust. His kingdom is righteous, and His reign will never end.
question: How could you bring your loyalty and trust to the eternal King this Advent?
prayer: O God, Your throne is for ever and ever, and the sceptre of Your kingdom is righteous. I give You my loyalty and trust, my eternal King. Amen.

text: Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him.
reflection: Psalm 72 is a prayer for the king, and it reaches toward a vision far beyond any earthly ruler: "Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him." Every king. Every nation. This is a picture of a universal kingdom. It points to Jesus, the King of kings. At His birth, wise men from the East came to bow before Him, an early fulfillment of this promise. And one day, every knee will bow and every tongue will confess that He is Lord. This verse also describes what kind of King He is. The surrounding verses say He delivers the needy, has compassion on the poor, and saves the lives of the oppressed. All nations will serve Him, not because He forces them, but because He is worthy. His reign brings justice and mercy. This Advent, join the wise men in worship. Bow before the King of all nations. And let His compassion for the needy shape how you celebrate this season.
question: How could the King's compassion for the needy shape the way you celebrate this season?
prayer: Lord Jesus, King of kings, all nations will bow before You. I join the wise men in worship, and I ask You to make me compassionate toward the needy this season. Amen.

text: And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots…
reflection: Isaiah uses a gardening image to describe the coming Messiah: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots." Jesse was the father of King David. By Isaiah's time, the royal family tree looked like a stump, cut down by judgment and exile. It seemed dead. But from that stump, God promised, a new shoot would grow. Life would spring from what looked lifeless. That shoot is Jesus, born in the line of David, in humble circumstances. God brought new life from a forgotten family tree. This is a message of hope for anyone who feels cut down. Perhaps your dreams have been cut off, your plans have failed, or your life feels like a stump. God specializes in bringing new growth from dead places. This Advent, bring your stumps to Him. Trust Him to bring forth a fresh shoot of life. The Branch from Jesse proves that God can make anything grow again.
question: What stump in your life looks lifeless, and can you trust God to bring forth new growth?
prayer: Lord, You brought a Branch from the stump of Jesse. I bring You the places in my life that look lifeless. Bring forth new growth, for You can make anything grow again. Amen.

text: And it shall be said in that day, Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the LORD; we have waited for him, we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation.
reflection: Isaiah looks ahead to a day of celebration: "And it shall be said in that day, Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the LORD; we have waited for him, we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation." Notice the repeated phrase: we have waited for him. Waiting is a major theme of Advent. God's people waited centuries for the Messiah. And when He came, the waiting gave way to joy. Waiting is hard. Many of us are waiting for something right now: healing, reconciliation, provision, answers. The waiting can feel endless. But Isaiah promises that the waiting is not in vain. One day, we will look up and say, this is our God. He came. He saved us. And our waiting will turn to gladness. This Advent, let your waiting be hopeful. Keep your eyes on God. Rejoice even now in the salvation He has already brought through Jesus, and in the salvation still to come.
question: What are you waiting for, and how can your waiting become hopeful this Advent?
prayer: Lord, this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He will save us. Make my waiting hopeful, and let me rejoice even now in Your salvation. Amen.

text: Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles.
reflection: God introduces His chosen Servant with tender words: "Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles." This Servant is upheld by God, chosen by God, delighted in by God, and filled with God's Spirit. And His mission is to bring justice to the nations. The following verses describe His gentle manner: He will not cry out loudly, a bruised reed He will not break, and smoking flax He will not quench. Matthew quotes this passage about Jesus. He is the gentle Servant who brings justice without crushing the weak. He is patient with the fragile and tender with the hurting. If you feel like a bruised reed or a flickering flame, this Servant will not break or extinguish you. He came to restore. This Advent, receive the gentleness of Jesus. Let Him uphold you, just as the Father upholds Him.
question: Where do you feel like a bruised reed or a flickering flame that needs Jesus' gentleness?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoking flax. Uphold me with Your gentleness, and restore what is weak in me. Amen.

text: And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.
reflection: God tells His Servant that His mission is too small if it only reaches Israel: "It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob … I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth." God's plan was always bigger. The Messiah would bring salvation not only to one nation but to the whole world. When Simeon held the infant Jesus in the temple, he echoed these words, calling Him a light to lighten the Gentiles. The child in the manger is the light of the world. This promise reaches you, wherever you are. The light of Christ shines to the ends of the earth. No one is too far away. This Advent, let His light shine on you. And then reflect it outward. Share the good news of Christmas with someone who may feel far from God. You can carry the light to the ends of your own world.
question: Who may feel far from God that you could carry the light of Christmas to?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are a light to the nations and salvation to the end of the earth. Let Your light shine on me, and help me carry it to someone who feels far from You. Amen.

text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
reflection: Isaiah paints a vivid picture of a messenger running across the mountains with good news: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!" The messenger's feet are dusty and tired, yet they are called beautiful because of the news they carry. Peace. Good. Salvation. God reigns. At Christmas, angels brought this same kind of news to shepherds: good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. And now we are called to be messengers too. Paul quotes this verse in Romans to describe everyone who shares the gospel. Your feet can be beautiful too. Every time you share hope, peace, or the good news of Jesus, you join this joyful procession. This Advent, look for an opportunity to bring good news to someone. Share a word of hope. Tell someone that God reigns, and that He came to save.
question: How could you bring good news to someone today, telling them that God reigns?
prayer: Lord, how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news. Give me an opportunity today to share a word of hope, and to tell someone that You reign. Amen.

text: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
reflection: Isaiah 53 describes the suffering Servant in some of the most moving words in Scripture: "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." Written centuries before Jesus, these words describe the cross with astonishing clarity. The child born at Christmas came to die. He would be wounded for our sins. He would bear the punishment that brings us peace. And by His wounds, we are healed. This reminds us that Christmas and the cross belong together. The manger and the cross are made of the same wood, as some have said. Jesus came not only to be with us but to save us, at great cost. This Advent, as you look at nativity scenes and sing carols, remember why He came. The peace of Christmas was purchased by His suffering. Receive His healing today. Let gratitude for His sacrifice fill your heart.
question: As you see nativity scenes and sing carols, how can you remember why He came?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You were wounded for my transgressions and bruised for my iniquities. Thank You for the peace You purchased with Your suffering. By Your stripes I am healed. Amen.

text: Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee.
reflection: Isaiah calls God's people to wake up: "Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee." The surrounding verses describe deep darkness covering the earth. But into that darkness, God's light has come. And His people are called not only to receive the light but to shine with it. At Christmas, the Light of the world was born. Into a dark and weary world, God sent His Son. And now everyone who receives Him is called to arise and shine. We are not the source of the light. We reflect His glory, like the moon reflects the sun. This Advent, perhaps you feel weary or surrounded by darkness. Hear God's call: arise. The light has come. You do not have to stay in the shadows. Let His glory rise upon you. And then shine. Let your kindness, joy, and hope reflect His light to those around you. The world needs to see it.
question: How could your kindness, joy, and hope reflect Christ's light to those around you today?
prayer: Lord, Your light has come, and Your glory has risen upon me. Lift me out of the shadows, and let me shine with Your kindness, joy, and hope. Amen.

text: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.
reflection: Through Jeremiah, God promised a new kind of king: "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth." Jeremiah lived when Israel's kings were corrupt and unjust. Leaders had failed the people. So God promised a righteous Branch from David's line. This King would do what earthly kings had failed to do: rule with perfect justice and righteousness. The very next verse gives His name: THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS. Jesus is that King. He is righteous in Himself, and He gives His righteousness to those who trust Him. In a world disappointed by leaders, this is good news. There is a King who will never fail, who will set all things right. This Advent, place your hope in Him. Whatever injustice troubles you, remember that the righteous King has come and will come again to bring justice to the earth.
question: What injustice troubles you, and how can you place your hope in the righteous King?
prayer: Lord Jesus, righteous Branch of David, You will execute judgment and justice in the earth. Whatever injustice troubles me, I place my hope in You. Amen.

text: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.
reflection: Zechariah calls for celebration: "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass." What a surprising King. He is just and brings salvation, yet He is lowly, riding not on a war horse but on a humble donkey. Five centuries later, Jesus fulfilled this prophecy as He rode into Jerusalem. But His humility began long before that. It began in Bethlehem, where the King of glory was born in a stable and laid in a manger. Jesus did not come with pomp and power. He came in humility, approachable to the poor and lowly. This means no one is too small or too ordinary to come to Him. Shepherds could visit Him. Children could climb into His arms. Sinners could eat with Him. This Advent, rejoice in your humble King. Come to Him without fear. He came lowly so that you could come near.
question: How does it help you to know that your King came lowly so that you could come near?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are just and bring salvation, yet You came lowly. I rejoice in my humble King, and I come near to You without fear. Amen.

text: Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts.
reflection: In the final book of the Old Testament, God makes a promise: "Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple." Two figures appear: a messenger who prepares the way, and the Lord Himself who comes. The New Testament identifies the messenger as John the Baptist and the Lord as Jesus. After Malachi, there were about four hundred years of prophetic silence. No new word from God. Yet the promise stood. And then, suddenly, an angel appeared to Zechariah in the temple, announcing the birth of John. The silence was broken. God was keeping His word. Perhaps you are in a season where God seems silent. You pray, but heaven feels quiet. Malachi reminds us that silence is not absence. God is still at work, preparing the way. And when His time comes, He arrives suddenly. This Advent, keep seeking Him. The Lord whom you seek will come.
question: Where does God seem silent, and how can you keep seeking Him while He prepares the way?
prayer: Lord, silence is not absence. When You seem quiet, help me keep seeking You, trusting that You are preparing the way and will come in Your time. Amen.

text: And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel.
reflection: When wise men arrived in Jerusalem asking about the newborn King, the religious scholars pointed to this prophecy: "And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel." Bethlehem was a small, unremarkable town. Yet God chose it as the birthplace of the King. What looked least became greatest because of who came from it. This is so often how God works. He chooses small places, ordinary people, and unlikely beginnings. He does not need impressive surroundings to accomplish His purposes. Perhaps you feel small or insignificant. Your town, your job, your life may seem ordinary. But God delights in using what the world overlooks. Little Bethlehem became the birthplace of the Savior. This Advent, take heart. God can do great things through small beginnings. And remember that the Ruler from Bethlehem came to shepherd His people with love.
question: What small beginning in your life could God use for something great?
prayer: Lord, You chose little Bethlehem as the birthplace of the King. Thank You that You do great things through small beginnings. Shepherd me with Your love. Amen.

text: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
reflection: When Jesus was baptized, the Father spoke from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Before Jesus performed a single miracle, preached a single sermon, or went to the cross, the Father declared His love and delight. Jesus did not earn His Father's approval through performance. He simply was the beloved Son. As we approach Christmas, this verse reminds us who the baby in the manger really is. He is the beloved Son of God, the One in whom the Father delights. And here is the astonishing news: through faith in Jesus, we are brought into that same love. We become beloved children of God. The Father's delight in His Son overflows to all who are in Him. Many people spend their lives seeking approval through achievements. But in Christ, you are already beloved. This Advent, rest in the Father's love. Hear His voice of delight over His Son, and know that through Jesus, that love reaches you.
question: Where are you still trying to earn approval, and how can you rest in being beloved through Jesus?
prayer: Father, Jesus is Your beloved Son, in whom You are well pleased. Thank You that through Him Your love reaches me. Help me rest in Your love instead of striving. Amen.

text: And there came a voice from heaven, saying, Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
reflection: Mark records the same moment at the baptism of Jesus, but with a personal touch. The Father speaks directly to the Son: "Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Not this is, but thou art. The Father addresses Jesus face to face, so to speak, with words of affirmation and delight. There is something intimate here, a glimpse into the eternal love between the Father and the Son. Before the world began, that love existed. And at Christmas, the Son left the glory of heaven to enter our world, still held in the Father's love. On this shortest day of the year for much of the world, when darkness lasts longest, this verse shines warmly. God's love is not cold or distant. It is personal and delighted. And through Jesus, God speaks words of love over His children too. Today, imagine the Father speaking directly to you through Christ: you are My beloved. Let that warmth fill the dark places of your heart.
question: What dark place in your heart could be warmed by hearing God say, "You are My beloved"?
prayer: Father, the love You have for Your Son reaches me through Christ. Let Your words of love fill the dark places in my heart, and help me live as Your beloved. Amen.

text: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised…
reflection: In His hometown synagogue, Jesus stood and read from Isaiah: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised." Then He sat down and said, today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing. This was His mission statement. Jesus came for the poor, the brokenhearted, the captive, the blind, and the bruised. Christmas is often portrayed as a season of abundance and happiness. But for many, it is also a time of grief, loneliness, and pain. Jesus came precisely for those people. His birth is good news for the broken. If you are hurting this season, know that Jesus came for you. He sees your pain. And if you are well, look around for the brokenhearted near you. Share the good news of Christmas in practical, compassionate ways.
question: Who around you is brokenhearted this season, and how could you share the good news with them?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You came to heal the brokenhearted and set the captives free. Meet me in my pain, and help me bring Your good news to those who are hurting. Amen.

text: The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.
reflection: John the Baptist saw Jesus walking toward him and cried out, "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." For centuries, lambs had been sacrificed in Israel. At Passover, a lamb's blood protected families from death. In the temple, lambs were offered for sin. But these sacrifices could never fully take away sin. They pointed forward to something greater. Now John points to Jesus and says: here He is. The true Lamb. The One whose sacrifice will take away the sin of the whole world. As we draw near to Christmas, remember that Jesus was born in a place where animals were kept. Perhaps lambs were nearby that night. And this newborn was the Lamb of God, born to be the final sacrifice. Christmas is not only about a baby. It is about the Lamb who came to take away your sin. Behold Him today. Look to Jesus, and let Him lift the weight of guilt from your heart.
question: What guilt could you let the Lamb of God lift from your heart today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, Lamb of God, You take away the sin of the world. I look to You today, and I ask You to lift the weight of guilt from my heart. Amen.

text: And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
reflection: On this Christmas Eve, Jesus offers us Himself: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst." It is fitting that Jesus was born in Bethlehem, a name that means house of bread. The One who would call Himself the bread of life was born in the town of bread and laid in a manger, a feeding trough. From the very beginning, He came to nourish us. Our souls are hungry. We try to fill them with many things: success, relationships, entertainment, possessions. These may satisfy for a moment, but the hunger returns. Jesus offers lasting satisfaction. When we come to Him, our deepest hunger is met. When we believe in Him, our thirst is quenched. Tonight, as many gather for Christmas Eve meals and services, remember the true Bread from heaven. Come to Jesus. Receive Him by faith. He alone can satisfy the hunger of your heart.
question: What hunger in your heart can only Jesus satisfy?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the bread of life, born in the house of bread. I come to You tonight with a hungry heart. Fill me with Yourself, and satisfy my soul. Amen.

text: Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
reflection: Merry Christmas! Today we celebrate the birth of the One who declared, "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life." On that first Christmas night, shepherds were watching their flocks in the dark. Suddenly, the glory of the Lord shone around them. Light broke into darkness. And that light was announcing the birth of Jesus, the Light of the world. Our world often feels dark. Suffering, fear, conflict, and grief cast long shadows. Many hearts are dark with loneliness or regret. But Jesus came to shine into all of it. He does not merely give light; He is the light. And He promises that those who follow Him will not walk in darkness. They will have the light of life. Today, as you celebrate with lights, candles, and gifts, remember the true Light who came. Follow Him. Let His light fill your heart and home. And share that light with someone who needs it.
question: How could you share the light of Christ with someone who needs it this Christmas?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the light of the world. Thank You for coming into our darkness. Fill my heart and home with Your light, and help me share it with someone who needs it. Amen.

text: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
reflection: The first people to hear about the birth of Jesus were shepherds. That seems fitting, because the baby they visited would grow up to say, "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep." Shepherds were often looked down upon in that culture. Yet God chose them to receive the first Christmas announcement. And Jesus chose the image of a shepherd to describe His love for us. A good shepherd knows his sheep by name. He leads them to green pastures. He protects them from danger. And this Good Shepherd goes further than any other: He gives His life for the sheep. The day after Christmas can feel like a letdown. The decorations, gifts, and gatherings are over. But the Shepherd remains. He does not leave when the celebrations end. He continues to guide, protect, and care for you. Today, rest in the care of your Good Shepherd. Follow His voice. He laid down His life for you, and He will never leave you.
question: How can you follow the voice of the Good Shepherd now that the celebrations are ending?
prayer: Lord Jesus, my Good Shepherd, You gave Your life for the sheep. Keep guiding, protecting, and caring for me after the celebrations end, and help me follow Your voice. Amen.

text: Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live…
reflection: Standing near the tomb of Lazarus, Jesus spoke to grieving Martha: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Jesus did not merely say that He could raise the dead. He said that He is the resurrection. Life itself is found in Him. Then He proved it by calling Lazarus out of the tomb. The baby born at Christmas is the One who conquers death. He came into our world of dying to bring life that never ends. For many, the end of the year brings reflection on loss. We remember loved ones who are no longer with us. The holidays can sharpen that grief. But this verse offers a hope stronger than death. Those who believe in Jesus will live, even though they die. Death is not the end of the story. Today, if you are grieving, bring your sorrow to Jesus. He wept at the tomb of His friend. And He is the resurrection and the life.
question: What grief could you bring to Jesus, who is the resurrection and the life?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the resurrection and the life. You wept at the tomb of Your friend. I bring You my sorrow, and I trust that death is not the end of the story. Amen.

text: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
reflection: On the night before He died, Jesus comforted His troubled disciples. When Thomas asked how they could know the way, Jesus answered, "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me." Jesus does not just show the way. He is the way. He does not just teach truth. He is the truth. He does not just give life. He is the life. Everything we need to come to the Father is found in Him. As one year draws to a close and another approaches, many of us think about direction. Where am I going? What is true? How can I truly live? Jesus answers all three questions with Himself. Follow Him, and you will not lose your way. Trust Him, and you will know the truth. Abide in Him, and you will have life. Today, as you look back on this year and ahead to the next, make Jesus your way, your truth, and your life.
question: As you look back on this year and ahead to the next, how can you make Jesus your way, truth, and life?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the way, the truth, and the life. As this year ends and a new one begins, help me follow You, trust You, and abide in You. Amen.

text: But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.
reflection: John tells us exactly why he wrote his Gospel: "But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name." John selected the miracles and teachings he recorded for one purpose: so that readers would believe and have life. The whole book is an invitation. Throughout this year, we have read hundreds of verses together. Each one is part of God's Word, written so that we might know Him, trust Him, and live. Scripture is not just information; it is invitation. It calls us to believe and receive life in Jesus' name. As the year closes, reflect on how God has spoken to you through His Word. Which verse stood out? Which promise carried you? Give thanks for the gift of Scripture. And if you have not yet placed your trust in Jesus, this is your invitation. Believe that He is the Christ, the Son of God, and receive life in His name.
question: Which verse from this year has shaped you most, and how can you give thanks for it?
prayer: Lord, thank You for Your Word, written so that I might believe that Jesus is the Christ and have life in His name. Let what I have read this year keep bearing fruit. Amen.

text: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
reflection: Peter and John stood before the religious council after healing a lame man. Boldly, Peter declared, "Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved." In a world with many religions, philosophies, and paths, this is a bold claim. Yet it is the clear message of the apostles. Salvation is found in Jesus alone. This is not arrogance; it is good news. God has not left us to find our own way to Him through endless effort. He has provided one sure way, open to everyone: the name of Jesus. Peter, a fisherman who had once denied Jesus, now proclaimed Him with courage. Grace had transformed him. As we near the end of the year, reflect on the wonder of this name. Jesus. Savior. The name above every name. Call on Him with gratitude. And share this good news with love and humility with those who are still searching.
question: How could you share the name of Jesus with love and humility with someone who is still searching?
prayer: Lord Jesus, there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. I call on Your name with gratitude, and I ask You to help me share it with love. Amen.

text: He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.
reflection: The Bible ends with a promise and a prayer. Jesus says, "Surely I come quickly." And John responds, "Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus." As this year comes to a close, we end with the same hope. Jesus came once, born in Bethlehem. And He has promised to come again. When He does, He will wipe away every tear, make all things new, and dwell with His people forever. This is the hope that has carried God's people through every year of history. It can carry you too. Whatever this year held, joys and sorrows, victories and losses, it is held within a larger story that ends in glory. Tonight, as one year ends and another begins, make John's prayer your own. Come, Lord Jesus. Come into my heart, my home, my new year. And come again to make all things right. Thank you for walking through this year of Daily Grace. May grace be with you today, tomorrow, and always.
question: What would it mean to pray "Come, Lord Jesus" over your heart, your home, and your new year?
prayer: Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus. Come into my heart, my home, and my new year, and come again to make all things right. Amen.
